title: From C++ source to execution: compilation, linking and debugging
lead: A source file is not executed directly. It goes through build stages, after which the program processes actual input.
why: When code fails to build or produces an incorrect result, identifying the stage of the problem is more effective than random edits.
objectives: Distinguish source, compilation, linking and execution.
Differentiate syntax, runtime and logic defects.
Support a fix with reproducible tests.

concepts.definition: Checking and translating C++ source into object representation.
Resolving cross-module symbols and dependencies into an executable.
The environment where a built program reads inputs and produces results.
Reproducing, locating, fixing and retesting a defect.

sections.title: Source files and builds
paragraphs: C++ is written in text files. A compiler handles source using selected language options, and diagnostic wording varies among tools.
Code Studio's actual capabilities depend on its runtime provider. Do not assume complete C++23 support merely from the tool name.

sections.title: Preprocessing, compilation and linking
paragraphs: Preprocessing handles directives such as #include. Compilation checks language constructs and translates code; linking resolves required symbols and libraries.
A missing semicolon typically causes a compilation error; a declared but undefined external function may cause a linker error.

sections.title: A program can fail after a successful build
paragraphs: Execution can encounter invalid input, forbidden operations and incorrect decisions. Integer division by zero must be prevented.
With two int operands, 10/3 is 3 rather than 3.333. This is the defined integer operation, not a compiler defect.

sections.title: Debugging starts with reproduction
paragraphs: Record the command, input, expected output, actual output and first relevant diagnostic. Classify the phase of failure before editing.
Make one motivated correction and rerun both the failing case and earlier successful cases.

sections.title: Standards and portability
paragraphs: Published C++23 is the normative language reference for this curriculum. In October 2026, C++26 remains under development and should not be assumed universally implemented.
The introductory course uses portable fundamentals. STL, exceptions, RAII and build systems require later targeted study and provider verification.

sections.title: A minimal reproducible example
paragraphs: A syntax defect prevents a build, for example a missing semicolon. An execution defect or wrong result appears when running: division by zero is invalid, while integer 10/3 yields 3 rather than 3.333. For negative integers, C++ truncates the quotient toward zero: -8/3 is -2. Save source, input, expected and actual output; fix one cause and rerun earlier tests.

sections.title: Input policy and execution limits
paragraphs: For the laboratory, a and b are limited to -1000000..1000000 and b must be nonzero. This also excludes quotient overflow.

Supply the stated number of whitespace-separated integer tokens. Extra tokens are outside this small input contract. Keep a record of source, exact stdin, predicted output and observed output. These examples introduce the logic; the following modules develop C++ types, streams and functions in depth.

workedExamples.title: Minimal runnable program
workedExamples.purpose: Connect C++ source to visible output.

workedExamples.title: Input validation and a bounded sum
workedExamples.purpose: Reject failed extraction and values outside -1000000..1000000 before addition. The accepted sum is within -2000000..2000000.
steps: Check both ranges before addition: successful extraction alone does not prevent overflow.
On failure print invalid and stop.
Otherwise add the bounded inputs and compare against the stated tests.

experiments.title: A syntax defect
experiments.action: Remove ; from a separate copy of the sample.
experiments.prediction: Compilation should fail; exact wording varies by provider.
experiments.verification: Record the diagnostic and restore the semicolon.

experiments.title: Integer division
experiments.action: Run the safe divider with 10 3 and 10 0.
experiments.prediction: The first result is 3; the second is invalid.

diagnostics.cause: The statement terminator is missing or the adjacent syntax is malformed.
diagnostics.fix: Inspect the reported location and repair the punctuation.

diagnostics.symptom: The program runs but the result is surprising
diagnostics.cause: The domain formula or integer-division semantics are misunderstood.
diagnostics.fix: Compare operator semantics and hand calculations.

practice.task: Classify syntax, linking, runtime and logic failures.
practice.criteria: Give an example and a diagnosis for each.

practice.task: Document a diagnosis of an incorrect order total.
practice.criteria: Include input, expectation, observation, hypothesis and regression evidence.
practice.hint: Change one cause at a time.

laboratory.title: Lab: safe integer division
laboratory.challenge: Read two integers; for invalid extraction or a zero divisor print invalid, otherwise print the integer quotient according to C++ semantics. For the laboratory, a and b are limited to -1000000..1000000 and b must be nonzero. This also excludes quotient overflow.
laboratory.starterCode: // Read a,b and check the input and b!=0 before dividing.
steps: Run the three Code Studio cases.
Explain integer truncation and rejection of zero division.
rubric: All listed reference cases match, including invalid and boundary inputs.
Submit source and a short test report.

assessment.question: When is a missing semicolon generally detected?
What is 10/3 when both values have type int?
What must be true before dividing a by b?

reflection: Why is successful compilation insufficient evidence of domain correctness?
What belongs in a useful defect report?
bridge: You are ready for systematic study of modern C++ syntax, types and engineering practices.

steps.description: Run the program with concrete input.

modulePracticum.title: Module project: a verifiable multi-item order
modulePracticum.challenge: Build a console program that validates a whole order, sums its items, calculates an integer discount and prints one reproducible result. Start with the requirement and tests, then implement and debug.
modulePracticum.readiness: Use this after all eight lessons. Functions and loops may be adapted from the provided starter; memorising syntax is not the goal. This project connects the reasoning skills of Module 1.
requirements: The header contains n and discount: integers, 0 ≤ n ≤ 20 and 0 ≤ discount ≤ 100.
Exactly n pairs follow: price and quantity, each an integer from 0 to 1000. Whitespace separates values.
Reject missing, nonnumeric, fractional or out-of-range values and extra non-whitespace input. Print only invalid followed by a newline; do not print a partial total.

subtotal is the sum of price × quantity for all items. saving = subtotal × discount / 100, rounded down; total = subtotal − saving. Print subtotal, saving and total separated by single spaces, then a newline.
For n = 0 the result is 0 0 0. The entire input still must satisfy the contract. Prices and totals use whole currency units, not floating-point money.
milestones: Write the input/output contract and predict the empty-order, 99-with-10%-discount and maximum-order results before opening the reference.
Draw a flowchart with success and failure branches. Write pseudocode, then split validation, item cost and discount saving into functions with preconditions and results.
Trace the three-item example using i, current item cost and subtotal. Explain the invariant: before iteration i, subtotal equals the cost of the first i validated items.
Implement the starter, run every listed case and record exact stdin, expected stdout, actual stdout and verdict. Add two of your own cases.
Reproduce and repair one defect, rerun earlier tests and explain why the evidence supports the fix.
walkthrough: For 120×3, 100×2 and 0×10 the accumulator changes 0 → 360 → 560 → 560. At each step it contains exactly the sum of the items already checked.
At a 15% discount, saving is 560×15/100 = 84 and total is 476. For 99 and 10%, saving is 9 and total is 90: rounding the final amount down instead would implement a different requirement.

long long is an integer type guaranteed to cover at least a signed 64-bit range. It keeps accumulation and multiplication separate from the narrower loop counter. Bounds still matter: at most 20×1000×1000 = 20000000 units are accumulated.

All output is deferred until validation is complete. std::ws consumes trailing whitespace; eof() checks that no other input remains. This is a stricter input contract than the small introductory examples.

i increases by one and cannot exceed n ≤ 20. That bound explains termination. The Euclidean lesson taught the same proof pattern: identify state, an invariant and a measure that moves toward stopping.

The starter compiles and prints todo. Its (void) lines only suppress unused-parameter warnings; replace each placeholder with the required calculation. Copying visible code does not replace your editor or mark the project complete.
artifacts: README.md — requirement, function contracts, pseudocode and flowchart.
trace.md — iteration table and invariant argument.
test-report.md — all listed tests, two additional cases and exact outputs.
debugging.md — failing input, hypothesis, change, retest and remaining limitations.

cases.purpose: Full discount on an empty order
Round the saving down before subtraction
Maximum item count, price, quantity and discount
Invalid item after a valid one: no partial total
Fractional suffix on the final value
Extra input is rejected by the contract
Apply the discount to the whole order, not separately to each item
Fractional header even for an empty order

rubric.complete: A precise contract, complete flowchart and matching pseudocode.
rubric.partial: One representation or an important boundary is missing.

rubric.complete: Function contracts, correct trace, invariant and termination argument.
rubric.partial: Implementation is split, but a contract or proof is incomplete.

rubric.complete: All invalid cases are rejected, no partial output, bounds and rounding are justified.
rubric.partial: The ordinary case works, but validation or rounding is incomplete.

rubric.complete: Every listed case and two additional cases have exact predicted and actual outputs.
rubric.partial: Tests exist but a category or evidence is missing.
rubric.missing: Only an unsupported claim that it works.

rubric.complete: A reproduced defect, tested fix and clear explanation of the algorithm.
rubric.partial: A fix is described without complete reproduction or retesting.

modulePracticum.completionRule: Self-check: at least 8 of 10 points, with no failure of required validation or a listed output. Use the rubric manually; it does not set a grade, mastery level or completion flag. A working reference alone is not your project evidence.
